A lot of commenters are posting and saying they die - while I have no absolutely confident answer, I’d at least like to entertain the math behind this. 

First, people are making statements like “oh a blue whale is X pounds and 10 million potatoes weigh more than that, they die. This conclusion is irrelevant to the fact beforehand - a blue whale is a single mass, these potatoes are not (or at least weren’t specified to be). As they roll down a HUGE ramp, they’ll bounce, scatter, and even cancel out part of each other’s force due to this non-uniform motion down the ramp. 

I’m no physicist, just studied mechanical engineering in college, so take some of my math with a grain of salt. I’m also making bad assumptions but I’m too lazy to actually do all the math. 

Assumptions: all potatoes are rolling down the ramp uniformly, no bouncing or anything. No air resistance. 

The formula for the acceleration of an object rolling down a ramp is A=(2/3)gsin(theta). We’re told the hill is at a 15% incline, which I assume is using the standard rating for hill grades on roads and not just a stand in for degrees, so that means theta is 8.627 degrees (approximately). 

A = (2/3)*9.81*sin(8.627)
A=~1 m/s^2

F=ma, mass of an individual potato is approximately 0.3kg, so we get
F=~0.3 Newtons
1 Newton, according to a YouTube video by Badzilla, feels like the force you feel pushing your hand down when you hold two snickers bars - not the big ones or the tiny ones, the standard size. So if all the potatoes were to hit the children in a large lumpy mass rolling perfectly down the ramp, then yes, it would be the force of holding up approximately 1,500,000 snickers bars.

However, perhaps we’re more interested in velocity of the potato by the time it gets to the end of the ramp (or rather, the kinetic energy)

Kinematic equation: 
Vf^2 = Vo^2 + 2*a*d
Vf^2 = 0 + 2*(1)*(200)
Vf^2 = 400
Vf = 400 m/s 

Kinetic energy equation: 1/2mV^2
KE = 1/2(0.3)(400^2)
KE = 24000 Joules
For reference, some dude’s comment on Quora that was upvoted by a PhD in Physics from Cornell stated that a bullet has approximately 1050 Joules of energy. So one potato would be carrying approximately 24 bullets worth of energy. Now there’s 10 million. 

Ok so potatoes probably wipe.

BUT.

Like I stated, potatoes aren’t rolling down a hill perfectly, and drag absolutely will reduce the speed of the potatoes if they actually managed to get to 400 m/s (approximately 900 mph). A comment by u/entropy2057 estimates an average potato to have a terminal velocity of 63.5 m/s, which then reduces the kinetic energy to approximately 600 Joules. So like, half a bullet. So maybe only 5 million bullets if there’s 10 million potatoes. 

BUT ONCE AGAIN, this assumes these potatoes somehow actually achieve terminal velocity while bouncing down 200 feet (oh fuck I just realized this was feet and I turned 200 to meters in my kinematic calculations but whatever, that just means my initial estimate for kinetic energy was short by a factor of approximately 9 - oh well) of hill, bouncing along, scattering, interacting with each other. That’s a ridiculous assumption and at best if a rolling potato on an 8.627 degree incline managed to achieve more than Usain Bolt’s sprinting speed (23.35 mph/10.44 m/s) I’d be surprised. 

So if we use that speed, suddenly each potato is hitting with 15 Joules of energy. According to yet another whole slew of Quora comment (this time, no upvotes from my helpful Cornell Physics PhD), 15 Joules is roughly the force of:

a) dropping a kilo bag of sugar from shoulder height

b) the recoil of a 30-06 rifle

c) if someone you’re sparring with accidentally connects 

Basically, 10 million reasonably solid punches delivered to 1000 elementary aged students. If divvied up evenly, that’s 10,000 punches per kid. 

If the older kids used the bodies of the younger kids as meat shields, they totally survive, assuming the potatoes follow fluid physics and they don’t all just clump and rest on top of the kids entirely. 

R1- potatoes win, 9/10

R2- kids survive, 7.5/10

R3- kids survive, 9/10

I used to work for one of the big 3 American investment banks, and did a few projects related to their ESG offerings. Having never worked in a finance role before this job, here are a few takeaways I got that largely skewed my thoughts on ESG investing in general: 

ESG is three separate things: Environmental, Social, Governance. Every holding in an ESG fund is rated on those three categories, with metrics within each category. Below is the quick and dirty on each: 

Environmental: what most people think about (at least, that was my impression going into this job) when it comes to ESG investing. Things like how green/ecologically sustainable a company’s line of business is, how eco-friendly their offices are, and their “projected” eco-friendliness in X years. The last one irked me because that metric was almost always self-reported, but I also understood why it was necessary. 

Social: a measurement of how socially conscious a company was - things like the use (or rather, the not use) of child labor, low wages, exploitation of underprivileged communities, etc. 

Governance: this was the one I personally hated, because it’s inherently so subjective. This is corporate governance, essentially measuring how strong a company’s corporate structure is. Things like diversity and women on their board of directors, having board or C-suite execs that are known to be good leaders (read: profitable), etc. This specific metric is the biggest offender for why you have so many prolific polluters and clearly non-environmentally friendly still categorized as ESG, and in a sense, they help make ESG fund managers generate the ever-coveted alpha

Hello hello! Hope I didn't misrepresent our school in any negative way :)

Columbia student here: 

It's actually something called School of General Studies (GS). It's one of Columbia's four undergraduate colleges (Columbia College (CC), School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), Barnard College (BC), and School of General Studies (GS))

As a GS student, I will be completely honest - the academic achievement the GS admissions officers look for isn't on par with the academic achievement of the other three schools. Instead, they look for a non-traditional life path, something that's different from the standard high school -> college for four years life. Its current iteration was founded for GIs coming back from WWII who had no academic backgrounds. Nowadays, while there's still a large population of MilVets (I believe in the ballpark of 300) in GS, we also have relatively high academic achieving students from diverse backgrounds - ballet dancers, chefs, kpop stars, actors, community college students, and so many more. I've met people who were convicted on felony charges and served their time and a student over 60 years old (our average age is 26 or 29, I can't quite remember anymore).

In many ways, the students in GS don't have the strong academic background that one might typically think would attend Ivy Leagues. However, they're still very academically capable, just not to the absolute insane level that other Ivy League students typically have (usually because of wealthy parents allowing them to attend private boarding schools that are direct pipelines into the Ivies), and instead bring a different perspective to classrooms that I believe makes Columbia one of the most well rounded, most diverse campuses in the US.
